\begin{highlightbox}
\textbf{KEY HIGHLIGHTS}
\begin{itemize}
  \item \textbf{The lead-time skill benchmark for Indian catchments.} Across 231 gauged catchments, drought-forecast skill vs climatology is large at a 1-month lead (median Brier skill score 0.42--0.50), collapses by 3 months (0.01--0.08), and is essentially zero at 6 months (at most 0.02). Persistence of the last observed index is the strongest baseline at every lead. Within our screened literature this is the first India-wide large-sample quantification of the seasonal drought-forecast ceiling, and it is the ceiling any operational or machine-learning system must beat.
  \item \textbf{The storage-state claim is tested and does not survive.} A recession-calibrated, mass-balance-verified storage-deficit state, pre-registered as the confirmatory family against the frozen best memory baseline, adds no skill at the 3- and 6-month leads (paired per-gauge Brier deltas of $-0.0015$ and $-0.0007$; positive in only 43\% and 41\% of gauges). The pre-registered parity prediction at the 1-month lead is confirmed exactly. The mechanism is measured, not assumed: median recession constants of about 8 days mean the fluid state is a smoothed mirror of information the indices already carry.
  \item \textbf{Two trustworthy nulls and a reusable verified engine.} A corrected re-run of the retired deficit-queue design (Gate G2) records that the queue loses to honest memory baselines; a power analysis shows that design was unresolvable at any sample size up to 300. All state estimation is verified by a 22-check battery, including a per-day mass-balance ledger and an analytic-recession agreement, and every number in this manuscript is generated by a committed script.
\end{itemize}
\end{highlightbox}

# Abstract (bullet form)

- **Background.** Seasonal forecasting of hydrological drought and low flows is a memory problem: fresh index observations decay while catchment storage persists (Sutanto \& Van Lanen, 2022). Whether a measured storage state adds forecasting skill beyond standard indices has not been tested at large sample in India.
- **Question.** Does a recession-calibrated storage-deficit state improve probabilistic forecasts of hydrological drought (standardised streamflow index, SSI-3, at or below $-1$) and low-flow events at 1, 3 and 6-month leads, beyond persistence, lagged indices and an antecedent precipitation index (API)?
- **Method.** One protocol on 231 Indian catchments (CAMELS-IND; 639 US catchments as a declared transfer check): per-catchment recession fits (baseflow index, recession constant, storage-outflow inversion for the storage scale), a fluid water balance with a per-day ledger, strictly prospective leads, six model families with cross-validated ridge penalties, a frozen per-gauge best-of baseline, and the Brier skill score (BSS) vs climatology as the headline metric (Table~\ref{tab:confirmatory}; Mangukiya et al., 2025; Kratzert et al., 2023).
- **Results.** Skill collapses with lead time (Table~\ref{tab:bss}; Figure~\ref{fig:leadtime}). The confirmatory contrasts fail at 3 and 6 months; the predicted parity at 1 month holds (Table~\ref{tab:confirmatory}).
- **Conclusion.** In these fast-draining monsoon catchments, standard indices already contain the usable memory; the realistic seasonal forecasting ceiling is now quantified, and the centre of gravity moves to climate-projection reliability (Singh et al., 2026).

# 1. Introduction

- Drought types have different defining variables and memory scales (Wilhite \& Glantz, 1985; Van Loon, 2015); hydrological drought integrates antecedent catchment state better than meteorological indices.
- The sub-seasonal to seasonal streamflow-drought forecasting literature is dominated by the United States and Korea (Hammond et al., 2025); within the literature we screened, no India-wide large-sample equivalent exists.
- The predecessor of this study modelled drought as a finite-capacity deficit queue; an external audit diagnosed three design causes for its null result (no information beyond the benchmark's own predictors; artefact queue mechanisms; a screen that selected on assumed constants) and the design was retired (PIVOT.md, 2026).
- **This paper asks the successor question with measured storage instead of assumed demand:** recession analysis estimates what the old parameters assumed (Brutsaert, 2008; Margreth et al., 2024).
- **Announced limitation (binding wording).** The storage state is estimated from precipitation, evapotranspiration and flow of the same catchment record that builds the indices; it is therefore a different transform with different memory properties, not independent information. The confirmatory question is exactly whether the physically-shaped transform out-predicts the standardised index transforms.

# 2. Data

- **India (primary):** CAMELS-IND daily catchment-mean precipitation, temperature and shipped GLEAM potential evapotranspiration, observed streamflow, and attributes including a measured irrigated fraction (Mangukiya et al., 2025). 472 gauges; 257 enter preparation; 231 pass the completeness screens (Table~\ref{tab:sample}).
- **USA (transfer check only):** Caravan-US forcings with FAO Penman-Monteith PET (Kratzert et al., 2023); the identical code path, reported descriptively, never as a contrast.
- Missing flow days are never interpolated; any month containing a missing day is excluded. Zero-flow days are kept as recorded and censored: recession segments start after the last zero-flow day and the storage state sits at its floor through a zero-flow spell. No gauge is dropped for a high zero-flow fraction alone.
- Training window 1981--2010; test window 2011--2020, touched once at scoring.

# 3. Methods

```{r figflow, fig.cap="Analysis flow from daily records to the frozen confirmatory contrasts. Every box is a script stage; the banner states the leakage rule that no threshold, screen, standardisation or fit touches a test year before scoring.", out.width="100%"}
knitr::include_graphics(FIG("Fig01_methods_flow.png"))
```

- **Recession fit (per catchment, training years only).** Baseflow index by a single-pass Lyne-Hollick filter (alpha $= 0.925$) with the smoothing constraint $b \le q$; recession segments of at least 10 consecutive days of strictly negative daily flow change with no rain day (at least 5 mm/day); recession constant $k$ as the median segment value of $\ln Q(t{+}1) - \ln Q(t) = -1/k$; low-flow exponent $p$ in $-dQ/dt = a\,Q^{p}$, clipped to $[0.5, 1]$ \[assumption: declared physical range\].
- **Storage scale.** With $Q_g = (K_a S)^{b_s}$ and $dS/dt = -Q_g$ along a recession, $b_s = 1/(2-p)$ and $K_a = a/b_s$; $S_{cap}$ is the 95th percentile of the implied storage over the training segments (Brutsaert, 2008). Catchments with fewer than 20 segments borrow basin-median parameters and are flagged.
- **Fluid state (daily, all rates in mm/day).**
  $$S(t{+}1) = \mathrm{clip}(S + P_e - E_a - Q_g,\ 0,\ S_{cap})$$
  $$P_e = \max(P - \varphi_m P,\ 0), \qquad E_a = \min(\mathrm{PET}\,K_{c,m},\ S + P_e), \qquad Q_g = \min\!\big((K_a S)^{b_s},\ S\big)$$
  Initialised at $S(0) = S_{cap}/2$ with a two-year warm-up excluded from features \[assumption\]. Observed discharge never enters as a daily input; it enters only through the fitted recession law and the censored zero-flow indicator.
- **Verification.** A 22-check battery pins the fluid engine three ways: analytic recession solution vs propagator vs per-day ledger identity $S(t{+}1)-S(t) = P_e - E_a - Q_g - \mathrm{overflow} + \mathrm{deficit}$ (residual tolerance $10^{-9}$), plus recession-constant recovery and storage-scale inversion on synthetic catchments.

# 4. Frozen study design

- **Targets.** T1 (confirmatory): monthly SSI-3 at or below $-1$, standardised on training years. T2 (descriptive): monthly mean flow below the training-period daily Q90.
- **Leads.** 1, 3 and 6 months, strictly prospective: a forecast issued at month $t$ uses only information available at $t$; every issue-target pair stays fully inside its window.
- **Families (identical ridge machinery, penalty tuned per family by calendar-block cross-validation inside the training years).** Climatology (reference); persistence (the target index at issue time); lagged indices (SPI-3, SSI-3, SSI-6, SPI-6 at issue time); API (recursive, decay 0.95); storage (state anomaly, 1- and 3-month storage change, days since high flow, and the fitted attributes); storage plus indices (the confirmatory family).
- **Confirmatory contrasts, frozen before scoring.** H1: storage-plus-indices vs the per-gauge best-of $\{$persistence, lagged indices, API$\}$ at the 3-month lead; H2: same at 6 months; the best-of is selected on training-year cross-validation only. H0 (descriptive, declared in advance): at the 1-month lead the storage family is expected to reach parity, and a null there is the predicted outcome.
- **Metrics.** BSS vs climatology (headline); paired per-gauge Brier deltas on identical held-out months; two-level block bootstrap (years within gauges, then gauges; 2,000 draws); one-sided sign test at at least 60 percent consistency; a declared harm bound of 0.005 Brier lists degraded gauges individually.
- **Class balance.** Cells with a training positive rate below 2 percent or above 98 percent are flagged and excluded from Brier contrasts.

# 5. Results

## 5.1 Sample

```{r tabsample, tab.cap="Sample report by screen stage. Source: results/p1_sample_report{,_usa}.csv.", tab.cap.style="caption"}
s <- num(TAB("table01_sample.csv"))
knitr::kable(s, format = "latex", booktabs = TRUE,
             caption = "Sample report by screen stage (India primary; USA transfer arm).",
             label = "sample")
```

- India: 257 catchments read, 231 pass the completeness screens, 218 pass the event-count screen for T1, and 136 additionally pass the recession-quality screen; 111 storage-family catchments borrow basin-median parameters. The working sample is an order of magnitude larger than the 12-gauge sample of the retired design.
- The USA transfer arm contributes 639 scored catchments.

```{r figmap, fig.cap="The screened sample across India, by screen stage (panel a). Red: storage-scored catchments; blue: completeness screens passed; grey: read but excluded.", out.width="88%"}
knitr::include_graphics(FIG("Fig02_study_map.png"))
```

## 5.2 The lead-time skill benchmark (Key highlight 1)

```{r leadtime, fig.cap="Lead-time skill curves (panel b), the centrepiece: median BSS vs climatology per family and lead. Skill collapses between the 1- and 3-month leads; persistence is the strongest baseline at every lead.", out.width="100%"}
knitr::include_graphics(FIG("Fig03_leadtime_skill.png"))
```

```{r tabbss, tab.cap="Median Brier skill score vs climatology per family, lead and target (India). Source: results/p1_bss.csv."}
b <- num(TAB("table03_bss.csv"))
knitr::kable(b, format = "latex", booktabs = TRUE,
             caption = "Median BSS (with interquartile range) per family, lead and target.",
             label = "bss")
```

- **KEY FINDING.** Forecast skill is large at one month (median BSS 0.42--0.50 across the memory families for the hydrological-drought target), collapses by three months (0.01--0.08), and is essentially zero at six months (at most 0.02). Persistence of the last observed index is the strongest baseline at every lead. This quantifies, for the first time at India-wide scale within our screened literature, the seasonal drought-forecast ceiling that any operational or machine-learning system must beat.

## 5.3 The confirmatory contrasts (Key highlight 2)

```{r tabconf, tab.cap="The frozen confirmatory decision table: storage-plus-indices vs the per-gauge best-of memory baseline on the SSI-3 target. H0 at the 1-month lead is the pre-registered parity prediction; H1 and H2 are the confirmatory tests. Source: results/p1_confirmatory.csv."}
cf <- num(TAB("table04_confirmatory.csv"))
knitr::kable(cf, format = "latex", booktabs = TRUE,
             caption = "Confirmatory contrasts (India): the frozen H0/H1/H2 decision table.",
             label = "confirmatory")
```

- **KEY FINDING.** H0 holds exactly as pre-registered: at the 1-month lead the storage family is at parity (median paired delta $-0.0003$; positive in 47 percent of gauges). The confirmatory tests H1 and H2 fail: medians $-0.0015$ and $-0.0007$, positive in only 43 and 41 percent of gauges, with two-level bootstrap intervals that do not support a positive effect.
- Against the API baseline alone the confirmatory family is ahead (median delta $+0.0044$ at 3 months; positive in 60 percent; sign test $p = 0.014$): the usable memory is in the standardised indices, not in raw rainfall memory.

## 5.4 Why: the state is a smoothed mirror of the record

```{r figstate, fig.cap="The mechanism (panel d): the ledger-verified storage state S(t) for catchment 13004 against observed flow (log scale) and precipitation. With a recession constant of about 8.5 days, the state drains within weeks and tracks the flow record's own memory.", out.width="100%"}
knitr::include_graphics(FIG("Fig05_example_state.png"))
```

```{r figlands, fig.cap="Storage landscape (panel e): fitted recession constants and storage scales across the sample; colour gives the baseflow index.", out.width="82%"}
knitr::include_graphics(FIG("Fig06_storage_landscape.png"))
```

- The fitted parameters explain the null mechanically: the median recession constant is about 8 days (Table~\ref{tab:params}), so the fluid state carries little memory beyond weeks, exactly the horizon where fresh indices are already strongest (Sutanto \& Van Lanen, 2022, find catchment memory pays where indices decay; these catchments' memory does decay).
- The exploratory post-hoc recession-speed cut (Table~\ref{tab:kclass}; clearly labelled, not confirmatory) shows no benefit even at 10--30-day recessions; only one catchment reaches the slow class.

## 5.5 Calibration

```{r figrel, fig.cap="Pooled reliability at the 3-month lead for the hydrological-drought target (panel f).", out.width="70%"}
knitr::include_graphics(FIG("Fig07_reliability.png"))
```

- Reliability is acceptable for all scored families; the collapse of discrimination, not miscalibration, is the binding constraint at seasonal leads.

## 5.6 Transfer arm (descriptive)

```{r tabusa, tab.cap="USA transfer check: descriptive best-of contrasts (no cross-region difference test is planned). Source: results/p1_summary_usa.csv."}
u <- num(TAB("table05_usa_transfer.csv"))
knitr::kable(u, format = "latex", booktabs = TRUE,
             caption = "USA transfer check (descriptive).",
             label = "usa")
```

- The US transfer arm mirrors the Indian pattern: near-parity at one month (median delta $+0.0007$; positive in 54.9 percent; sign test $p = 0.012$) and no gain at 3 or 6 months. The protocol transfers; the null transfers with it.

## 5.7 Power and the retired design (Key highlight 3)

```{r figpow, fig.cap="Sign-test power at 0.60 consistency from the Gate-G2 variance (panel g): no sample size up to 300 could have resolved the retired concurrent design.", out.width="80%"}
knitr::include_graphics(FIG("Fig08_power.png"))
```

```{r tabpow, tab.cap="Sign-test power from the Gate-G2 variance (normal approximation for the improvement probability; declared). Source: results/p1_power.csv."}
pw <- num(TAB("table06_power.csv"))
knitr::kable(pw, format = "latex", booktabs = TRUE,
             caption = "Sign-test power at 0.60 consistency.",
             label = "power")
```

- The corrected re-run of the retired deficit-queue design (Gate G2) is recorded as a null: with dataset PET, a measured irrigated fraction, training-only thresholds and the honest memory baselines added, the queue loses to the best baseline (USA median paired delta $-0.0059$, 95 percent interval $[-0.0187, +0.0026]$; positive in 25 of 60 gauges).
- At that effect size the sign-test power at 0.60 consistency is below 0.03 for every sample size up to 300 (Table~\ref{tab:power}): the retired concurrent design was unresolvable by construction, which is the audit's FS2 diagnosis converted into a measurement.

# 6. Discussion

- **For operators.** In these catchments a seasonal drought outlook beyond one month currently has almost no index-based skill to build on; the honest ceiling is now measured, and persistence should be the declared reference forecast for any claimed improvement.
- **For the machine-learning frontier.** Streamflow-drought forecasting benchmarks of the Hammond et al. (2025) type do not yet exist for India at large sample; this study supplies the baseline distributions (BSS by lead, family and target) that any India-wide learned system must be compared against, with the leakage discipline and paired statistics to make the comparison fair.
- **For the storage-state hypothesis.** The negative result is mechanism-backed: fast monsoon recessions bound the memory any storage transform built from P, ET and Q can carry. A genuinely independent storage observation (groundwater levels or total water storage) is the remaining route, and is recorded as future work.
- **Limitations.** The announced limitation stands: the storage state is a different transform of the same record, not independent information. The seasonal demand curves are declared simplifications. The gate decision for the retired design rests on its screened sample (5 and 60 gauges); the power analysis, not the point estimate, carries that conclusion.

# 7. Conclusions

- The lead-time skill benchmark for Indian catchments is established: large skill at one month, collapse by three, zero at six; persistence is the reference to beat.
- A recession-calibrated, mass-balance-verified storage state adds no forecasting skill beyond the indices in this data; the pre-registered parity prediction is confirmed and the seasonal-skill claim is retired with its mechanism measured.
- The verified engine, battery and protocol transfer unchanged to the next study: transient deficit probabilities and recovery-time distributions under four climate scenarios on the same 472 catchments (Singh et al., 2026), where no benchmark contest exists and the quantities themselves are the product.

# Appendix A. Reproducibility

- **Folder layout.** `paper01/` contains this manuscript (`MANUSCRIPT_Paper01.Rmd`, knitted to `MANUSCRIPT_Paper01.pdf`), `figures/` (Fig01--Fig08, PDF and 300-dpi PNG), `tables/` (Table 1--5 and appendices, CSV with JSON provenance sidecars), `results/` (frozen copies of the study outputs with sidecars), and `figure_table_captions.md`.
- **One command each.** Figures: `Rscript R/figures_paper01.R`. Tables: `Rscript R/tables_paper01.R`. Verification battery: `Rscript R/verify.R` (22/22 required). The study itself: `Rscript R/study_p1.R` (India plus transfer arm) and `Rscript R/study_gate_g2.R` (gate).
- **Every number is generated.** All in-text statistics are knitted from the frozen tables in `paper01/tables/`; the tables are written by script from `paper01/results/`, which are frozen copies of `output/*.csv` carrying JSON sidecars (git hash, code hash, shape, R session). Nothing is hand-edited.
- **Split discipline.** Training years 1981--2010 for every threshold, screen, standardisation, recession fit and tuning; test years 2011--2020 touched once at scoring; the leakage tripwire is battery check V20.

# Appendix B. Declared assumptions

- Lyne-Hollick alpha $= 0.925$ (single pass, smoothing constraint $b \le q$).
- Rain-day threshold 5 mm/day; segment length at least 10 days; at least 20 segments per gauge (else borrowing).
- Storage-outflow inversion: exponent $p$ clipped to $[0.5, 1]$; $S_{cap}$ as the 95th percentile of implied storage over training segments.
- Fluid state: $S(0) = S_{cap}/2$; two-year warm-up excluded; missing climate inputs enter as zero and their months are excluded by the complete-month rule.
- API decay 0.95 (effective memory about 90 days); ridge grid $\{0.1, 0.3, 1, 3, 10\}$ with five contiguous calendar-year-block folds.
- Harm bound 0.005 Brier (smallest season-scale change an operator would act on).
- Power analysis uses a normal approximation for the improvement probability at the Gate-G2 effect size.
